volumes.title_en: Beyond the Palace: The Secret Garden
volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Changdeokgung Palace, Seoul
volumes.category: History › Asia › Korea
volumes.collection: Palaces — Where Time Rests (궁궐 — 시간이 머무는 곳)
volumes.description_en:
Beyond the palace walls, the Secret Garden of Changdeokgung waits in silence.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Changdeokgung Palace — a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the heart of Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, the garden becomes a space where time lingers — where now and not-now coexist. Autumn sunlight pauses on the pond before drifting away. A solitary pavilion rests behind ancient trees. Visitors pass like shadows, and branches bathed in light stand in quiet witness.
Built in the 15th century, Changdeokgung Palace remains one of Korea's most intimate royal spaces. Its Secret Garden — the Huwon — was shaped not for spectacle but for contemplation. This volume approaches the garden not as history, but as lived time: the still water of Buyongji, the seclusion of Aeryeonjeong, and the quiet halls of Yeongyeongdang.
The Korean Photo Essay Series (KPE Archive) is a long-form photographic archive documenting emotional time across Korean landscapes. Season I: Coming and Going Time comprises 30 individual photo essays and 10 thematic collections, 2026.
“This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.”
This volume marks the first chapter in an ongoing archive of emotional time.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Changdeokgung Palace in Autumn Rain, Seoul
volumes.category: History › Asia › Korea
volumes.collection: Palaces — Where Time Rests (궁궐 — 시간이 머무는 곳)
volumes.description_en:
Autumn rain settles over the Secret Garden, and the palace breathes more slowly.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Changdeokgung Palace — a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the heart of Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, rain becomes its own language. Drops gather on the still face of Buyongji, streams gain strength along the eaves, and the zelkova stands darkened and patient. Mallards drift across a soaked pond while visitors move beneath a grey, low sky — every surface softened, every sound hushed.
Tucked along the slope of Bugaksan, the Secret Garden of Changdeokgung was made for stillness rather than display. In the rain its pavilions and ponds turn inward, and the garden reveals a different season of feeling: Buyongji under a steady shower, Yeonghwadang in the wet, and Aeryeonji veiled by falling water.
The Korean Photo Essay Series (KPE Archive) is a long-form photographic archive documenting emotional time across Korean landscapes. Season I: Coming and Going Time comprises 30 individual photo essays and 10 thematic collections, 2026.
“This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.”
This volume continues the Secret Garden sequence — the same place, seen through the weather of memory.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Gyeongbokgung Palace, Seoul
volumes.category: History › Asia › Korea
volumes.collection: Palaces — Where Time Rests (궁궐 — 시간이 머무는 곳)
volumes.description_en:
Even across five hundred years of memory, time continues to flow through the royal palace.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Gyeongbokgung Palace — the principal palace of the Joseon dynasty, in the heart of Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, the grand palace turns intimate. Wind passes over open courtyards, lotus leaves rest on the water before Gyeonghoeru, and light moves slowly across Sujeongjeon. Visitors come and go beneath vast roofs, small against the centuries, carrying their own quiet stories.
As the principal palace of the dynasty, Gyeongbokgung has stood at the center of Korean history — built, burned, and raised again. This volume approaches it not as monument but as flowing time: the reflecting pavilion of Gyeonghoeru, the scholar's hall of Sujeongjeon, and the long courtyards where the present and the past keep passing through one another.
The Korean Photo Essay Series (KPE Archive) is a long-form photographic archive documenting emotional time across Korean landscapes. Season I: Coming and Going Time comprises 30 individual photo essays and 10 thematic collections, 2026.
“This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.”
This volume turns from the Secret Garden to the great palace at the city's heart.

volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Snow — Silence After Footsteps (설경 — 발자국 이후의 침묵)
volumes.description_en:
On the day the first snow falls, the village grows even quieter.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Eunpyeong Hanok Village, beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, winter settles over the tiled roofs one flake at a time. The first snow softens the lanes, the hanok eaves carry a thin white line, and the village seems to hold its breath. Each frame lingers on the hush between falling and fallen — the moment a place becomes still.
At the foot of Bukhansan in Jingwan-dong, Eunpyeong Hanok Village gathers traditional Korean houses against the mountain's ridgelines. In snow it sheds its postcard brightness and turns inward — courtyards, walls, and rooflines reduced to quiet shapes, a contemporary village remembering an older way of being still.

Light shifts slowly over the snowfield, and the pavilion stands as a single quiet form between earth and winter sky.
Yongchuljeong rises as the symbol of Eunpyeong Hanok Village, where the ridgelines of Bukhansan meet the rooftops below. Under snow the hill becomes a field of soft blossoms, and the pavilion — built for pause and prospect — turns into a place to measure stillness rather than distance.

A quiet photographic meditation set in Gijachon Village, beneath Bukhansan in Jingwan-dong, Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, a single snow path leads beneath the hill and into stillness. Footprints, fences, and bare branches gather under falling snow; the slope rises softly into white. Each frame follows the quiet of walking — the way a familiar place turns unfamiliar, and tender, under the first heavy snow.
Nestled beneath Bukhansan in Jingwan-dong, Gijachon was once home to journalists and has slowly faded at the city's edge. In snow its lanes and low houses become a path of memory — a vanishing village held for a moment in white, walked rather than viewed.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Gijachon and Umulgol, Seoul
volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Time — Moments That Overlap (시간 — 겹쳐지는 순간)
volumes.description_en:
Once, more than five hundred households shared these lanes; now wild grass grows where autumn leaves come and go.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Gijachon and Umulgol, beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, two timelines flow side by side. Leaves arrive and fall along a built walking path; a few ginkgo trees still stand firm where houses once stood. Flowers come, leaves turn, and a peaceful emptiness settles over the slope.
Built between 1969 and 1974, Gijachon was Korea's first residential community for journalists — more than 500 households in its narrow lanes. Today a new town has risen around it, and the old village lingers at the edge, half-remembered, as autumn keeps passing through.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Sangnim Village and Pokpodong, Seoul
volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Time — Moments That Overlap (시간 — 겹쳐지는 순간)
volumes.description_en:
On Mount Imal, where court ladies and eunuchs lie at rest, the living and the dead dwell together.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Sangnim Village and Pokpodong, beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, life and death share a single hillside. Between old gravestones the barefoot living pass quietly by; one life watches another; a trace remains where fear once moved. The village unfolds slowly, holding presence and absence in the same frame.
Sangnim Village takes its name from a single juniper — the “Sang Tree” — that once stood at Jingwan-nae-dong, beside an old well where neighbors gathered. On the slopes of Mount Imal, the resting places of court ladies and eunuchs overlap with the everyday life of the living, and time itself seems to fold.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Eunpyeong Hanok Village and Jegakmal, Seoul
volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Time — Moments That Overlap (시간 — 겹쳐지는 순간)
volumes.description_en:
A hanok village where past and present stand side by side, and three philosophies once shared a single hillside.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Eunpyeong Hanok Village and Jegakmal, beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, the past and the present rest together. On one patch of grass lies a descendant of a king; across the stream, Buddhist prayer rises on the mountain slope. Tiled roofs hold the memory of filial devotion while today's village goes quietly about its day.
Before the tiled roofs of today's Eunpyeong Hanok Village, this land was called Jegangmal, named for royal ancestral shrines once built here. The teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism were passed down together — and their traces still linger where past and present coexist.

This volume lingers where the village's past and present keep each other company.

volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Walks — Between Leaving and Returning (산책 — 떠남과 돌아옴 사이)
volumes.description_en:
From high above the apartments, I watched the traces of the departed scatter along the stream.
A quiet photographic meditation set along Gongneungcheon, on the northern edge of Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, a stream becomes a river of time. Walking paths, railway lines, and quiet water carry memory southward. Seen from above, the everyday turns tender — a place to walk a while with someone who has gone before, and to glimpse, in the ordinary, the back of a feeling once held.
Gongneungcheon rises in the hills of Goyang and moves south through the northern edge of the city before joining the Han River. Along its banks lie footpaths and old railway traces — an ordinary waterway that, walked slowly, becomes a passage through memory.

volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Bulgwang-dong and Changneung Stream, Seoul
volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › New Age & Spirituality › Mindfulness
volumes.collection: Walks — Between Leaving and Returning (산책 — 떠남과 돌아옴 사이)
volumes.description_en:
Beneath pale streetlights, only passing figures remain, and the alleys quietly fade from view.
A quiet photographic meditation set in Bulgwang-dong, along Changneung Stream beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, darkness keeps its small secrets. Figures pass without a glance; a crescent moon lingers, then moves on; old signboards go on naming shops that may soon be gone. In alleys unsettled by redevelopment, the ordinary takes on the tenderness of things about to disappear.
Bulgwang-dong — “the place touched by Buddha's light” — sits at the foot of Bukhansan, where temples once shaped the rhythm of daily life. Today the neighborhood is changing, and along Changneung Stream the old passages quietly give way, noticed by almost no one.
The Korean Photo Essay Series (KPE Archive) is a long-form photographic archive documenting emotional time across Korean landscapes. Season I: Coming and Going Time comprises 30 individual photo essays and 10 thematic collections, 2026.

This volume walks the fading alleys, attentive to those who pass without notice.

I used to look broadly; now I look through a narrow gap, and the near and the far come together as one.
A quiet photographic meditation set along the road to Bulgwangsa and Bulgwang Neighborhood Park, beneath Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, walking slows until distance dissolves. Through the narrowest gap, nearness and farness quietly meet; vague memories appear gently; the fruit of time grown in indifference is seen anew. Each frame is a step taken without hurry.
At the foot of Bukhansan, in the quiet folds of Bulgwang-dong, the road climbs toward Bulgwangsa, beside Bulgwang Neighborhood Park where legend and stillness share a single hill. Here a slow walk becomes its own kind of seeing.

volumes.collection: Temples — The Shape of Stillness (절집 — 비움의 자리)
volumes.description_en:
When lotus lanterns bloom among brilliant spring flowers, the temple windows glow with quiet prayer.
A quiet photographic meditation set at Jingwansa, deep in the folds of Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, lantern light and blossom share the same air. Paper lanterns drift in rows above the courtyard; petals settle on stone; the old halls hold their stillness as spring moves softly through.
Founded in the early Goryeo period and sheltered in mountain light, Jingwansa is one of Seoul's enduring temples — a place where prayer has continued for a thousand years. In spring it fills with lotus lanterns, and the sacred and the seasonal quietly overlap.

volumes.title_en: The Seat the Monk Left Behind
volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Samhwasa Temple, Seoul
volumes.category: Religion & Spirituality › Buddhism › Zen / Chan
volumes.collection: Temples — The Shape of Stillness (절집 — 비움의 자리)
volumes.description_en:
Silence fills the emptied seat, and time is made whole through letting go.
A quiet photographic meditation set at Samhwasa, hidden deep in the folds of Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, absence becomes presence. An empty cushion holds the shape of the one who left; light rests on worn wood; the small hermitage keeps a silence deep enough to forget the city below.
Beyond the familiar path to Jingwansa, hidden deeper in the mountain, stands Samhwasa — small enough to miss, quiet enough to forget. Founded by a nun in the late 1950s, it remains a hermitage of returning silence, where what is absent speaks as clearly as what remains.

volumes.description_en:
Even the thousand-year stone Buddha flows; impermanence is not grief but grace.
A quiet photographic meditation set at Samcheonsa, on the slopes of Bukhansan in Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, stone and wind keep an old conversation. A wind chime trembles at the eaves; water echoes faintly in the valley; the rock-carved Buddha gazes out, weathered and serene, beyond the reach of the visible.
On the slopes of Bukhansan, Samcheonsa keeps an older memory — tradition traces it to the Silla monk Wonhyo, and the Goryeosa records its monks across the centuries. Carved into stone and into time, it holds the long patience of a place that has watched everything pass.

Among Seoul's palaces, Changgyeonggung feels closest to spring. Built as a residence for royal elders, it carries a gentler intimacy than the grander palaces — and when spring fully blooms, its ponds and pavilions soften into color and shade.

On the island where immortals were said to wander, a passerby pauses her steps.

Through HongSahn's lens, water and concrete learn to rest. Vines climb the old tanks; reflections gather in still basins; a passerby pauses, youth whispers nearby, and the island holds many ages of life at once.
Once a water treatment plant, Seonyudo was reborn as a garden where industry softened into green. Along the river's slow breath, it rests like a quiet pause in the city — a place where immortals were once imagined to play, now open to anyone walking slowly.

Even after five hundred years, the bond between mother and son remains unbroken.
A quiet photographic meditation set at Taegangneung Royal Tomb, in the pine-scented hills of Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, the royal tombs keep their long silence. Pine shadows fall across stone guardians; grass bends in the wind; two burial mounds rest near one another, holding a bond that time has not loosened.
In the quiet hills of Gongneung-dong lie two royal tombs — Taereung and Gangneung — joined in name and memory. Though crowns have long since passed, the tie between mother and son endures here, kept in stone and pine across five centuries.

volumes.title_en: Bond of Mother and Child II
volumes.subtitle_en: A Photographic Meditation on Uireung Royal Tomb, Seoul
volumes.category: History › Asia › Korea
volumes.collection: Royal Tombs — Names That Stay in Earth (왕릉 — 이름이 머무는 곳)
volumes.description_en:
The mother steps forward and asks, moved by pity for the son who stood alone and left the world too soon.
A quiet photographic meditation set at Uireung Royal Tomb in Seokgwan-dong, Seoul. This is not a guide to Korea. It is a way of feeling it.
Through HongSahn's lens, sorrow settles softly over stone. Light moves across the burial mounds; the guardians keep their watch; a quiet harmony of grief and devotion lingers in the still, ordered ground.
Nestled in Seokgwan-dong, Uireung holds the tombs of King Gyeongjong and his queen — a place of quiet sorrow. Gyeongjong's brief and solitary reign ended early, and here the bond of mother and son finds its second telling, in a tragic, tender harmony.
